name: Phase Four: The Six Week Pilot
title: Phase Four: The Six Week Pilot
answer: Phase Four is a six week pilot in which two or three volunteer teachers use a new AI tool as designed, track one main measure before and after, and meet on a date set in advance to decide what happens next. It matters because six weeks is long enough to reveal a pattern and short enough to stop without regret, and because a pilot that includes a curious but skeptical teacher and a comparison group gives the school more believable evidence about whether the tool actually helped.

sections.body: The six week pilot is a bounded trial meant to replace open ended experimentation with a clear decision. It uses two or three teachers who volunteered, asks them to use the tool as designed, and expects honest reporting. The problem it solves is that schools can adopt tools on enthusiasm alone and then struggle to tell whether anything changed. By setting one main measure before the tool arrives and recording it again at the end, the pilot creates a before and after picture. It also sets the decision meeting date before the pilot begins, so the school commits to deciding rather than drifting.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the pilot starts with two or three volunteer teachers and one main measure recorded before the tool is introduced. The teachers use the tool as designed and report honestly, and the pilot closes with a decision meeting on a date chosen in advance. The text does not give separate grade bands, so the same structure applies wherever the tool is used. To make the result more useful, the school can compare three classrooms using the tool with three similar classrooms that do not, which helps show whether the change came from the tool or from something else such as the time of year. If a comparison group is not possible, the baseline carries more weight, and for any tool students use to practice, the pilot needs a check done without the tool, such as a short paper quiz, a conversation, or a task completed without AI.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label to the six week pilot, so the design rests on practice rather than research. It does point to Chapter 1, which showed how practice scores can rise while real learning falls. That finding is the reason the pilot includes a check done without the tool, so the school can see whether students learned or simply performed better with help. The text also refers to Figure 4.5, which lays out the six week template. No study, sample size, or numerical result is given in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The pilot has limits that the text sets out. Volunteers make pilots run smoothly, but a pilot staffed only by the most enthusiastic users will tell the district little about how the tool works for everyone else, so including at least one curious but skeptical teacher makes results more believable and helps spot problems enthusiasts overlook. A comparison group may not be possible, and when it is absent the baseline has to carry more of the weight. Results should be written down before anyone decides whether they liked the tool, which keeps personal preference from taking over. The decision meeting date is set before the pilot begins, and the choice of what to do next stays with the people in that meeting rather than with the tool.
